records.expert_reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding record the replication outcome as 'successful'. Under Codebook Rule 1, the authors state a clear overall positive verdict on their conceptual replication of Hygen et al. (2014): competitive model-fitting across both primary (kindergarten) and secondary sensitivity (Grade 6 and linear/continuous) analyses supported the hypothesized model, with the overall patterning of the data matching all four a-priori predictions (divergent positive and negative behavior between disorganized Met carriers and Val/Val homozygotes, no genetic differences among organized children, and relationship specificity to maternal rather than teacher reports). While the authors note that Hygen et al. (2014) found the interaction for change over time whereas the present study intentionally tested levels of functioning, they explicitly conclude that 'The data from the both the primary and sensitivity analyses fit the Hygen et al. (2014) hypothesis' and that 'reasonably consistent support for the Norwegian hypothesis emerged in both inquiries'.
records.label: objection
records.reason: The expert calls support for the Norwegian hypothesis an overall replication verdict, but the full Discussion explicitly contrasts the original empirical result (interaction predicted change, not levels) with the present significant levels result. Agreement with a hypothesis is not by itself a whole-replication verdict overriding that original-specific contrast. The mother-only specificity agrees; the levels/change comparison differs. This requires parent outcome review rather than certification of successful under Rule 1; a smaller interaction alone is not the objection.

7   Conclusion

Acharya and Pedersen (2005) study the effect of liquidity risk on the cross-section
of asset returns and develop the LCAPM formula with the four testable hypotheses
that (1) the intercept term is zero, (2) the illiquidity costs have a positive effect,
(3) the net liquidity risk also has a positive effect, and (4) the market risk premium
is equal to the liquidity risk premium.
    This paper tests the validity of the AP LCAPM for six models, eight test portfolios,
and three different datasets (the 1964 to 1999 US data, the recent 2000-16 US
data, and the 1978-2012 Japanese data). We find that the AP LCAPM satisfies the
one-variable LCAPM test for 36.0% of 64 regressions and the two-variable LCAPM
test for 5.2% of 96 regressions. These results are consistent with Holden and Nam
(2018).
    Although the idea of the liquidity risk that investors are concerned with the
fluctuation of liquidity over time is very economically intuitive, when there are
severe multicollinearity among the illiquidity costs, the market beta, and the
liquidity betas, the estimation results are statistically unstable and hard to interpret.
